problemText: In his 1493 letter to Luis de Santángel, Christopher Columbus describes the islanders he encountered as "guileless, and so liberal of all they have that no one would believe it." Paired with his description of Española's fertile land and gold-bearing rivers in the same letter, this characterization of the people mattered chiefly because it —
choices: framed the land and the people as resources ready for colonization
confirmed to European readers that the islanders had already converted to Catholicism before Columbus arrived
proved that Columbus had negotiated a formal, lasting peace treaty with the islands' rulers
warned Spanish investors that further voyages to the islands would likely prove unprofitable
hints: Notice that Columbus published this account to convince backers, like Luis de Santángel, to keep funding voyages.
Read the description of the people alongside the description of the land — both are framed the same way.

problemText: Columbus's 1493 letter to Luis de Santángel describes Española's harbors and rivers, "most of them bearing gold," as surpassing "anything that would be believed by one who had not seen them." This letter shaped later European colonization primarily because it —
choices: was addressed directly to King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella, who personally financed the voyage
was suppressed by the Spanish Crown to prevent rival powers from learning of the discovery
was printed and circulated across Europe within months, building support for further voyages
accurately catalogued the exact quantities of gold Columbus's crew had already collected
hints: The letter was addressed to a royal treasury official, not the monarchs themselves — think about what happened to it after that.
Ask whether this passage reads like a private report or something meant for a wide audience.

problemText: Bartolomé de las Casas describes how, after conquest, Spanish colonists "divided among themselves the Young Men, Women, and Children reserved... one obtained thirty, another forty, to this Man one hundred were disposed, to the other two hundred," then sent the men to the mines "to dig and bring away the Gold" while the women worked the fields. This passage documents the operation of which Spanish colonial system?
choices: The repartimiento, a system of rotational labor drafts administered directly by colonial officials
The casta system, which classified colonial society by ancestry and birthplace
The Valladolid debate, a formal Crown-convened argument over Native treatment
The encomienda, granting colonists the right to demand Native labor and tribute
hints: This system grants fixed numbers of people to individual named colonists — that is different from a rotating labor draft run by officials.
Recall which labor system came first, before the Crown shifted toward rotational drafts.

problemText: In "A Brief Account of the Destruction of the Indies," Las Casas rejects Spain's official justifications for colonization, writing that the Spaniards came "not for the Honour of God... nor to serve the King, as they falsely boast and pretend to do," but "stimulated and goaded on by insatiable Avarice and Ambition, that they might for ever Domineer, Command, and Tyrannize over the West-Indians." This passage is best used as evidence of —
choices: the final abolition of the encomienda system as a direct result of Las Casas's writings
an internal Spanish debate over colonization, not proof his advocacy ended forced Native labor
a consensus among Spanish colonists that conquest could never be morally justified
the Spanish Crown's official position that colonization existed solely to enrich the royal treasury
hints: Las Casas's advocacy led to real but partial reform (the New Laws, 1542) — did it end forced labor entirely?
This passage is a Spanish churchman arguing against Spain's own official rationale — think about what that shows about Spanish opinion, not what it changed by itself.

problemText: In his 1520 letter to Charles V, Hernán Cortés describes Tenochtitlan's great market as "twice as large as that of Salamanca," with "more than sixty thousand souls, buying and selling" there daily. Coming from the Spanish conqueror who would help destroy the city the following year, this description is most valuable to historians as evidence that —
choices: Cortés intended his letters to convince Charles V to abandon further conquest in the Americas
Native economies relied entirely on subsistence agriculture with no organized trade or markets
Tenochtitlan's population and trade networks were smaller than contemporary Spanish accounts assumed
pre-conquest Mesoamerican societies had built large, economically sophisticated urban centers
hints: Ask what kind of city could support a market with tens of thousands of daily buyers and sellers.
This account comes from the very man who conquered the city — consider why his description is still useful evidence.

problemText: The Codex Mendoza, commissioned around 1541 by Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza, records the tribute — bundles of woven cotton mantles, quilted cotton warrior costumes, and loads of maize — that conquered provinces owed their Aztec rulers, compiled to inform Spanish colonial administration. That a Spanish viceroy commissioned this detailed tribute record most directly illustrates —
choices: how Spanish colonial administration extracted resources from Native peoples by adapting existing tribute structures
how the Spanish Crown replaced every indigenous form of taxation with an entirely new European system
how the Valladolid debate persuaded Spain to abolish tribute demands on conquered provinces
how the encomienda system was formally abolished once the Codex Mendoza was completed
hints: The tribute categories recorded (cotton mantles, feathers, maize) are the same kinds of goods Aztec rulers had already been collecting before the conquest.
Ask why a Spanish colonial official would want a careful record of what provinces already owed in tribute.

problemText: In "A Discourse Concerning Western Planting" (1584), Richard Hakluyt argues that Spain and Portugal's overseas discoveries had given them "so many honest wayes to set them on worke, as they rather wante men then meanes to ymploye them," while England, lacking colonies, "cannot deliver our commonwealthe from multitudes of loyterers and idle vagabondes." Hakluyt's argument here most directly illustrates that —
choices: English colonization was organized around the same encomienda-style labor grants Spain used in the Americas
European powers pursued colonization for varied motives, not one shared model
Spain and Portugal had eliminated poverty at home entirely because of their overseas colonies
English colonization began only after the Valladolid debate settled the treatment of Native peoples
hints: Hakluyt is comparing England's problem with idle, unemployed people to how Spain and Portugal supposedly solved the same problem.
This motive (employment) is different from Spain's encomienda-style labor extraction — European colonizers did not all colonize for the same reasons or in the same way.

problemText: Before 1492, the Mississippian center of Cahokia (near present-day St. Louis) reached a population estimated as high as 10,000-20,000 people, supported by intensive floodplain maize agriculture, while Pacific Northwest maritime societies built large, socially stratified communities without practicing any agriculture at all. Together, these two societies serve as evidence against which claim about pre-contact North America?
choices: that Mississippian and Pacific Northwest peoples were unified under a single political authority
that Mississippian and Pacific Northwest societies shared an identical political structure based on the potlatch
that pre-1492 North America was a sparsely populated wilderness shared by one uniform Native culture
that Mississippian and Pacific Northwest societies both first emerged only in the centuries just before European contact
hints: One of these societies farmed intensively; the other had no agriculture at all — what does that difference already disprove about a single 'Native culture'?
Think about the two-part myth this unit pushes back on: an empty continent, and one shared way of life.

problemText: Which constitutional amendment, ratified in 1920, granted women the right to vote nationally?
choices: The Eighteenth Amendment, which banned the manufacture and sale of alcohol
The Nineteenth Amendment
The Twenty-First Amendment
The Seventeenth Amendment
hints: Two of the other amendments listed deal with alcohol, not voting rights.
This amendment was ratified the same year the decade begins.

problemText: The Eighteenth Amendment, ratified in 1919 and taking effect in January 1920, banned the manufacture and sale of alcohol nationwide. Which outcome most directly explains why it was repealed just thirteen years later?
choices: The Supreme Court ruled the amendment unconstitutional in 1925 after several state governments challenged its enforcement powers in court
European governments imposed trade sanctions in retaliation for the ban
Rural voters organized to protect a whiskey-based export economy
It proved unenforceable, fueled organized crime, and cost the government badly needed tax revenue during the Depression
hints: Think about what happened to drinking once it was banned outright — did it stop, or move underground?
Consider what the federal government was losing in revenue just as the Depression hit.

problemText: The Harlem Renaissance flourished in New York during the very same decade that Southern states enforced strict Jim Crow segregation and the revived Ku Klux Klan reached several million members. This timing is best explained by which development?
choices: the Great Migration concentrated Black artists, writers, and musicians in Northern cities where Jim Crow's legal segregation did not take the same form
Congress passed a sweeping federal law during the 1920s specifically funding and integrating Black artistic institutions nationwide
the Ku Klux Klan's decline after 1925 opened new economic opportunities for Black artists across the South
Jim Crow laws were formally struck down in New York State in the early 1920s, ending all forms of racial segregation there entirely and immediately
hints: Ask where the Great Migration (1915-  ) actually sent hundreds of thousands of Black Southerners, and why that mattered for where this cultural movement could take root.
No federal arts-funding law or New York State desegregation law of this kind existed in the 1920s — the real explanation is about population movement, not new legislation.

problemText: A historian argues that the 1920s' surface prosperity concealed structural problems that would surface in the 1929 crash. Which piece of evidence BEST supports this argument?
choices: The Immigration Act of 1924 sharply increased the number of low-wage industrial workers, flooding factories with workers willing to accept even lower wages than before
Ku Klux Klan membership collapsed after 1925, easing social tensions in rural areas
Agricultural commodity prices stayed depressed throughout the decade even as urban consumer spending and stock speculation surged
The Scopes Trial proved that most Americans rejected the theory of evolution
hints: The 1924 Immigration Act actually cut immigration sharply — it didn't add workers.
Look for evidence that a whole sector of the economy was NOT sharing in the 'roaring' prosperity.

problemText: Which 1954 Supreme Court case declared state-mandated public school segregation unconstitutional, overturning the doctrine of 'separate but equal'?
choices: Plessy v. Ferguson
Brown v. Board of Education
Loving v. Virginia, the 1967 case striking down bans on interracial marriage
Korematsu v. United States
hints: Plessy is the OLDER case this one overturned, not the answer itself.
This case is named for a Kansas school-segregation lawsuit.

problemText: In February 1960, four Black college students sat down at a whites-only Woolworth's lunch counter in Greensboro, North Carolina, and refused to leave when denied service. What did this tactic demonstrate about the movement's evolving strategy?
choices: College students had abandoned nonviolent tactics in favor of armed self-defense
The March on Washington had already achieved integrated public accommodations before 1960
The NAACP's legal strategy had become unnecessary once federal troops began enforcing Brown in every Southern school district by the late 1950s
Organizers were shifting from litigation alone toward direct, nonviolent confrontation that could spread rapidly to other cities
hints: The sit-in itself was strictly nonviolent — no weapons involved.
The March on Washington happened in 1963, three years AFTER this sit-in.

problemText: During the 1963 Birmingham campaign, television cameras broadcast police attacking peaceful Black demonstrators, including children, with fire hoses and police dogs. Civil rights leaders had calculated that this kind of violent response would —
choices: discredit the movement in the eyes of most Northern white viewers, a reaction organizers considered unlikely given the movement's national visibility
provoke Congress to authorize immediate military occupation of the South
generate national outrage that built pressure for federal civil rights legislation
convince the movement's leadership to abandon nonviolent tactics entirely
hints: Think about who was watching on television, and how they likely reacted to seeing children attacked.
This event is widely linked to the passage of a major law the very next year.

problemText: The Civil Rights Act of 1964 outlawed discrimination in employment and public accommodations. Why was a separate Voting Rights Act still needed in 1965?
choices: The 1964 Act left the literacy tests, poll taxes, and other tactics still barring Black Southerners from voting untouched
The 1964 Act had already been struck down by the Supreme Court in a ruling handed down the previous year
The 1964 Act applied only to Northern states, exempting every state south of the Mason-Dixon line from its provisions
The Fifteenth Amendment had already been repealed by that point
hints: The 1964 Act's focus was jobs and public accommodations — check what it left untouched.
No constitutional amendment guaranteeing Black voting rights was ever repealed.

problemText: John Winthrop's 1630 sermon describing the Massachusetts Bay colony as a 'city upon a hill' expressed the Puritan belief that their community would serve as —
choices: a profitable trading post independent of any religious purpose, entirely apart from any religious mission
a temporary refuge before the settlers returned to England
a moral example whose righteousness the world would watch
a religiously neutral haven open to all faiths equally
hints: 'City upon a hill' is a visibility metaphor — something everyone can see and judge.
The Puritans intended to stay and build a permanent, godly community, not go home.

problemText: New England town meetings, in which property-owning men voted directly on local matters, are best understood as —
choices: an early democratic practice that planted seeds of American self-government, even though participation was limited
proof that colonial New England had achieved full democracy for all residents, a level of participation historians do not consider genuinely universal
a religious ritual with no real political function
a system copied directly from Virginia's plantation government
hints: Notice the qualifier: only property-owning MEN could vote — that limits how 'full' this democracy was.
Virginia's colonial government was organized very differently, around large landholders and an appointed governor.

problemText: Historians link the Great Awakening (1730s-40s) to the American Revolution because revival preachers' message — that ordinary people could find salvation directly, without relying on an educated clergy — most directly —
choices: established the Anglican Church as the sole legal religion enforced uniformly across every New England colony
ended all religious revivalism in the colonies after roughly 1750
united the colonies under a single Puritan denomination
encouraged colonists to question institutional authority, including political hierarchy, decades before independence
hints: If ordinary people can bypass religious authorities, what other kind of authority might they start to question?
Think about the gap in time between the Awakening (1730s-40s) and independence (1776) — this is about a long-term effect, not an immediate one.

problemText: Roger Williams was banished from Massachusetts Bay in 1636 for arguing for separation of church and state and fair treatment of Native Americans, then founded Rhode Island on principles of religious toleration. His banishment is best used as evidence that —
choices: Puritan New England sought religious liberty for all residents, including dissenters
the Puritans pursued religious freedom for their own community, not universal toleration for dissenting beliefs
Massachusetts Bay had no religious establishment capable of enforcing conformity
Rhode Island was founded before Massachusetts Bay as a haven for Puritans, years after Williams's own banishment from that colony
hints: Williams was punished for the very views Rhode Island would later be founded on — what does banishing him show about Massachusetts's own tolerance?
Massachusetts Bay was founded in 1630, six years before Williams was banished and founded Rhode Island.

problemText: The Indian Removal Act of 1830 led directly to which event, in which thousands of Cherokee died during a forced march to present-day Oklahoma?
choices: The Trail of Tears
The Nullification Crisis, the 1832-33 standoff between South Carolina and the federal government over tariffs
The Bank War
King Philip's War
hints: This event is named for the suffering of the forced march itself.
The other three options involve tariffs, banking, and a much earlier colonial conflict — none involve forced relocation.

problemText: Jackson vetoed the recharter of the Second Bank of the United States in 1832, arguing it served wealthy elites rather than ordinary citizens. What was a direct consequence of shutting down the Bank?
choices: An immediate return to the gold standard that stabilized the currency
The founding of the Federal Reserve System later that same decade
Unstable state-issued currency that contributed to the Panic of 1837
South Carolina's nullification of the federal tariff
hints: Without a national bank regulating currency, who issued money instead, and how reliable was it?
The Federal Reserve wasn't created until 1913 — long after Jackson's presidency.

problemText: In Worcester v. Georgia (1832), the Supreme Court ruled that Georgia could not extend its laws over Cherokee territory. Jackson's response to this ruling illustrates —
choices: the Supreme Court's ability to directly enforce its own rulings without executive cooperation, a power the Constitution reserves for Congress and the states acting together, not the courts alone
Jackson's consistent deference to judicial decisions throughout his presidency
a rare instance of judicial and executive power operating in perfect alignment
the president's willingness to defy a Supreme Court ruling he disagreed with, weakening the Court's practical authority in that instance
hints: Courts have no army or police of their own — they depend on the executive branch to enforce their rulings.
Jackson proceeded with Indian removal despite this ruling — what does that tell you about enforcement?

problemText: Historians describe the expansion of white male suffrage under Jackson as genuine but bounded. Which piece of evidence BEST illustrates this qualification?
choices: Property requirements for voting were eliminated for all adult residents regardless of race or sex, a change that in practice applied only to men who already met the old property qualifications
Nearly all white men gained the vote by the 1830s, while women, Black Americans, and Native Americans remained excluded
The spoils system extended government employment to women for the first time
The Nullification Crisis proved that federal authority had become irrelevant to Southern states
hints: 'Bounded' means the expansion helped some groups but not others — which groups were left out?
The spoils system rewarded political supporters with government jobs, not a specific demographic group like women.

problemText: Reagan's 1980s political program combined tax cuts and deregulation with which foreign-policy posture toward the Soviet Union?
choices: Détente and gradual disarmament negotiations only, a posture Reagan explicitly rejected as insufficient to pressure Soviet reform toward openness
Formal recognition of Soviet territorial claims in Eastern Europe
A renewed Cold War hard line, including the Strategic Defense Initiative and pressure at the Berlin Wall
Withdrawal of all US nuclear forces from Europe
hints: Reagan called for Gorbachev to 'tear down this wall' — that's not a soft, accommodating posture.
SDI (the 'Star Wars' missile-defense program) was a major buildup, not a withdrawal.

problemText: NAFTA (1994) and China's 2001 entry into the World Trade Organization both reflect which broader trend in the 1990s-2000s US economy?
choices: Accelerating globalization, expanding trade even as domestic manufacturing employment declined
Increasing economic isolationism and rising tariff barriers, a posture neither agreement reflects given their tariff-reducing purpose
A shift back toward an agrarian economic base
The elimination of income inequality through free trade
hints: Both NAFTA and WTO entry are about REDUCING trade barriers, the opposite of isolationism.
Expanded trade with lower-wage countries put pressure on which sector of the US economy specifically?

problemText: After the September 11, 2001 attacks, the PATRIOT Act is best understood as an example of —
choices: a peacetime reduction in federal law-enforcement power, the opposite of what Congress actually did in response to the attacks
a treaty ratified by the United Nations Security Council
a temporary measure repealed within a year of passage
expanded federal surveillance and law-enforcement authority justified by the new counterterrorism priority
hints: Think about what a government typically does with its own powers right after a major attack on its soil.
This was a domestic US law passed by Congress, not an international treaty.

problemText: Historians point to the 2008 financial crisis as a key turning point in recent US politics primarily because it —
choices: restored broad public confidence in the effectiveness of both major political parties
fueled populist backlash on both the right (Tea Party) and left (Occupy), eroding trust in elite institutions
ended American military involvement in the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq
led directly to the ratification of a new constitutional amendment placing federal examiners inside every major national bank
hints: Look for movements that emerged AFTER 2008 on both ends of the political spectrum.
No new constitutional amendment on banking was ratified after 2008 — Dodd-Frank was ordinary legislation, not an amendment.

problemText: The 1494 Treaty of Tordesillas, mediated by the Pope, divided newly claimed non-European territory primarily between which two powers?
choices: England and France
the Netherlands and Spain
Portugal and England
Spain and Portugal
hints: This treaty came right after Columbus's voyages, which were sponsored by Spain.
Portugal had already been exploring the African coast and Atlantic islands before 1492.

problemText: In the century following 1492, Native American populations in many regions of the Americas declined by an estimated 50 to 90 percent. Which factor was the PRIMARY driver of this decline?
choices: Epidemic disease introduced by Europeans, against which Native populations had no prior immunity
Intertribal warfare that intensified independent of European contact
Voluntary migration of Native peoples to Europe
crop failures caused by Old World grazing livestock destroying Native maize fields across the continent
hints: This decline happened even in areas Europeans had barely reached in person — how could that be, unless something spread ahead of them?
'Virgin soil epidemic' is the term historians use for this — no prior exposure means no immunity.

problemText: The Spanish colonial casta system, which classified colonial society by degrees of European, Indigenous, and African ancestry, differed from the racial system that later developed in British North America chiefly because it —
choices: enslaved only Indigenous peoples under a legal system that formally excluded anyone of African descent
granted full legal equality to all colonial subjects regardless of ancestry, treating every casta category identically under Spanish law
recognized and ranked a wide range of mixed-ancestry categories rather than sorting the population into a strict binary
was abolished immediately after the Valladolid debate
hints: Casta paintings depicted MANY named categories of mixed ancestry — count how many labels existed versus a simple 'Black/white' split.
The Valladolid debate addressed the treatment of Native peoples, not the casta classification system itself.

problemText: Spanish colonization in the Caribbean and Mexico relied heavily on extracting labor and tribute from dense, already-settled Native populations through the encomienda system. French colonization of the St. Lawrence valley, by contrast, centered on —
choices: large-scale plantation agriculture worked by an enslaved labor force, a model the French pursued only briefly before abandoning it entirely
the fur trade conducted through alliances with Native nations, with comparatively light settlement
an encomienda-style tribute system imposed on Native communities
mass immigration of entire European families seeking farmland
hints: French colonization in Canada involved far fewer settlers than Spanish or later English colonization — think about why.
Encomienda was a specifically Spanish institution — France pursued a different economic relationship with Native nations.

problemText: Which constitutional amendment, ratified in 1870, prohibited denying the right to vote on the basis of race?
choices: The Fifteenth Amendment
The Thirteenth Amendment, ratified five years earlier, in 1865
The Fourteenth Amendment
The Nineteenth Amendment
hints: The Thirteenth ended slavery and the Fourteenth granted citizenship — this one comes after both.
The Nineteenth Amendment is about a different group's voting rights, ratified 50 years later.

problemText: The Freedmen's Bureau, established in 1865, provided formerly enslaved people with which combination of services?
choices: Direct cash payments of forty acres and a mule to every freed family
Full voting rights enforced by federal troops in every Southern county
Schools, food, legal aid, and help negotiating labor contracts
Permanent land grants confiscated from all former Confederate officers
hints: 'Forty acres and a mule' was a famous but largely undelivered promise, not the Bureau's actual mandate.
The Bureau was chronically underfunded — think about what modest services it could realistically provide.

problemText: The contested 1876 presidential election was resolved by an informal deal in which Republicans secured the presidency for Hayes in exchange for —
choices: ratifying the Fifteenth Amendment
appointing a Southern Democrat as Chief Justice
admitting several new Western territories as free states in exchange for continued Southern Democratic cooperation
withdrawing federal troops from the remaining occupied Southern states, ending Reconstruction enforcement
hints: The Fifteenth Amendment was ratified years earlier, in 1870 — before this compromise.
This deal is remembered as the event that effectively ENDED Reconstruction — what would achieve that?

problemText: A student argues that Reconstruction 'completely failed' because Jim Crow segregation followed within two decades of its end. Which fact complicates this claim?
choices: The Thirteenth, Fourteenth, and Fifteenth Amendments remained part of the Constitution and later became the legal foundation for the twentieth-century civil rights movement
The Freedmen's Bureau continued operating without interruption through the 1950s
Congress readmitted no former Confederate states until after 1900
The Compromise of 1877 restored full federal enforcement of Black voting rights, the opposite of what actually happened once the deal was reached in 1877
hints: The Freedmen's Bureau actually shut down in 1872 — it did not last anywhere near that long.
The Compromise of 1877 did the OPPOSITE of restoring enforcement — it withdrew troops.

problemText: Which of the following crops originated in the Americas and, after 1492, became a staple food across much of Northern Europe?
choices: Wheat
Sugarcane, brought from the Old World to Caribbean plantations
The potato
Rice
hints: Wheat, sugarcane, and rice all moved the OPPOSITE direction — from the Eastern Hemisphere into the Americas.
This crop grew well in poor, cold soil and helped fuel population growth across Ireland and Eastern Europe.

problemText: The Columbian Exchange transferred crops and livestock in both directions across the Atlantic, yet its demographic consequences were overwhelmingly one-sided. Which statement best explains this apparent contradiction?
choices: Old World diseases devastated Native American populations, who lacked prior immunity, while New World crops mainly enabled population growth in Afro-Eurasia rather than causing losses there
New World crops such as maize and the potato caused a population decline across Europe fully comparable in scale to the disease-driven demographic collapse across the whole of the Americas
The exchange of livestock, unlike crops or disease, moved exclusively from the Americas to Europe and never in the reverse direction
Native American populations in the continent's deep interior were largely unaffected because epidemic disease spread only along the coasts
hints: Crops and disease both moved, but did they move in the SAME direction, and did they have the SAME effect wherever they landed?
Disease often traveled ahead of European settlers themselves, along existing Native trade networks — it was not limited to coastal contact zones.

problemText: The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) Confederacy united five nations under the Great Law of Peace before sustained European contact. Which feature of Haudenosaunee political organization is most notable for the political authority it gave to women?
choices: A monarchy in which only women could inherit the throne
A system in which only unmarried women could vote in council meetings, a structure no Haudenosaunee nation actually used
An entirely female governing council with no male participation
Matrilineal clans in which women held a voice in selecting male chiefs
hints: The Confederacy had no monarchy at all — it was a council-based alliance of nations.
Chiefs were still male; the notable feature is who had a say in choosing them.

problemText: Ancestral Puebloan communities in the arid Southwest built irrigated agriculture and multi-story stone dwellings, while Haudenosaunee communities in the Northeast built a political confederation among five nations. Considered together, these two societies best support which conclusion about pre-1492 Native America?
choices: Political confederation was the single dominant, universally shared form of government among nearly all Native societies regardless of environment or region
Native societies developed solutions closely adapted to their own environment and needs, not one shared model
Agriculture was practiced identically across every region of North America
Only Southwestern societies achieved permanent, complex settlements
hints: One of these societies is defined by irrigation farming, the other by political alliance — they solved very different problems.
The Haudenosaunee were in the Northeast, not the Southwest, and reached complexity through political organization, not irrigation.
